I'm not a legal expert, so take this with a grain of salt, but the semantics here are important. Tor provides anonymity; it can provide privacy, but only when used properly. Despite the similarity in the concepts there are really important differences between the two.

Privacy means that you can't see my actions. Anonymity means that you might be able to see my actions but can't tie them to me. So for instance, if I am sitting at a table with a barrier suspended a foot off of it with writing supplies on the other side, someone on my side of the table could see me, but would not be able to see that I was writing or what I was writing. I have privacy in regards to person 1. Person 2 is on the opposite side of the barrier and can only see my hands writing. I have anonymity in regards to person 2.

Anonymity is usually a critical step in achieving privacy, but the two are not the same.

The judgement says that the defendant had no reasonable expectation of either privacy or anonymity so the judge is still wildly mistaken in regards to privacy, but the article title is misleading at best.
